rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With contextual indications, the answer to the conditional clause lawlā can be omitted; the translation supplies its implication.
rows.anchor: In the presence of concomitant indications

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sending a messenger was favor and warning to Quraysh and the Ishmaelites: it prevented their excuse that no messenger had come and made the truth conclusive.
rows.anchor: This is an expression of God’s favour on the Quraysh or, in other words, on the Ishmaelites.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human intellect and innate guidance suffice to guide people; punishing those who ignored that innate guidance would not violate justice.
rows.anchor: the light of intellect and innate guidance found in human nature is sufficient to guide him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Messengers provide further conclusive communication, leaving no excuse; God's established practice is to destroy every nation that denies its messenger.
rows.anchor: from the face of the earth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-haqq denotes both the Book and God's Messenger, which are essentially one; min ʿindinā stresses the truth's exalted source, so opposition to it is evil and doomed.
rows.anchor: here connotes both the Book and the Messenger of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi attributes Quraysh's demand for Moses-like miracles to Jewish scheming to incite them against Muhammad; Quraysh repeated the objection without seeing the scheme.
rows.anchor: Concomitant indications show that this objection was spread by the Quraysh, but it was planted in their minds by the Jews.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The attribution of the objection reflects inward similarity: like Pharaoh's people, Quraysh were arrogant and acted accordingly; the preceding allusion to Jewish prompting sharpens the eloquence.
rows.anchor: Verbs and pronouns are very commonly used in Arabic in this way.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the two magicians is an exaggerated expression, comparable to saying “Zayd is justice.”
rows.anchor: Yet an element of exaggeration is incorporated in the sentence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taẓāhara means mutual cooperation or connivance; Pharaoh's people accused Moses and Aaron of joining forces.
rows.anchor: The word تَظٰهَرَ means mutual co-operation and connivance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Pharaoh's people meant they would reject both Moses and Aaron and all their miracles, however forcefully the two presented them.
rows.anchor: however much these two forcefully presented their miracles, they would not profess faith in them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is to challenge them to bring a divine book with better guidance than the Qur'an and Torah, promising to follow it if they are truthful.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) was ready to follow it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their appeal to Moses is only an excuse to evade guidance: they follow neither Moses nor Muhammad and genuinely accept neither the Torah nor the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: the enthusiasm they were showing to support Moses (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeking guidance is intrinsic to upright human nature; Muhammad believed in both the Torah and Qur'an, with the latter offering greater guidance.
rows.anchor: this very requirement of human nature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an affirms the Torah and rejects only its interpolations; it offers sounder guidance because it cleanses revelation, completes it, and fulfills the Torah's prophecy.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ ān does not refute the Torah: it attests to it. Its refutation is confined to the interpolations found in it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who leave God's guidance to follow their own whims are farther from guidance than anyone else.
rows.anchor: those who want to follow their own whims leaving aside God’s guidance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Desires cannot distinguish truth from falsehood or good from evil, and can overpower a person's intellect.
rows.anchor: between truth and falsehood, good and evil and at times they are so forceful

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Success requires following desires in the light of God's guidance; following them without that light leads to doom.
rows.anchor: the way to success for a person is to follow these desires in the light of God’s guidance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God revealed guidance to save people from destruction by their desires; those who submit to blind desires wrong themselves and, by God's established practice, are deprived of guidance.
rows.anchor: Such people are ones who are unjust to their souls

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God maintains an unbroken succession of guidance; when the Torah's bearers became indifferent, He blessed Muhammad with His guidance.
rows.anchor: It has always remained in force.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This restates 28:45–46: the Qur'an is familiar, not alien; the People of the Book should accept God's favor now perfected, and the Ishmaelites should welcome the direct favor given them without a prior messenger or book.
rows.anchor: This is actually a re-statement of the topic discussed earlier in verses 45 and 46.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those previously given the Book refers to its righteous People, as Islahi explains that an active-voice verb used for them here denotes the pious among them.
rows.anchor: This verse actually points to a testimony

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Righteous People of the Book testify to the Qur'an's truth and accept it, so their response should outweigh the aversion of their miscreant compatriots.
rows.anchor: there were also the righteous People of the Book

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their emphatic confession shows heartfelt recognition that the Qur'an's accounts of earlier scriptures are true; they also urge Quraysh's leaders to honor it rather than invite doom by opposing it.
rows.anchor: these people from the depth of their hearts attested to the contents

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their claim to have believed beforehand refers to prophecies about the Qur'an in their scriptures; “Muslimīn” shows they awaited and then submitted to this Messenger and Book.
rows.anchor: they believed in the Qur’ ān even before its revelation because of the prophecies found about it in their own scriptures.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their double reward is for remaining faithful to Moses' religion amid their nation's deviation, then eagerly awaiting and joyfully accepting the final Prophet and perfect religion foretold by Moses, Jesus, and other prophets.
rows.anchor: a special reason for referring to their trait

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Perseverance matters because they endured hardship to keep their former religion and then faced opposition from their own people and Quraysh after accepting Islam; Simon's followers suffered under self-styled innovators.
rows.anchor: they had to face the opposition of both their own nation and of the Quraysh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥasana means steadfastness and forgiveness; al-sayyiʾa denotes opponents' objections, allegations, abuse, and insults, to which the believers respond decently and forgivingly.
rows.anchor: means steadfastness and forgiveness and

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wealth-lust obstructed the People of the Book, especially Jews, from accepting Islam; the sūrah's Qarun, Jesus' saying, and Abu Lahab illustrate greed's role in resistance.
rows.anchor: the greatest impediment for the People of the Book

rows.speaker: Jesus (sws)
rows.claim: Jesus is quoted as saying that a rich person entering God's kingdom is harder than a camel passing through a needle's eye.
rows.anchor: Jesus (sws) is reported to have said

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their charitable spending shows these righteous people escaped greed and avarice, which helped make them fortunate enough to accept Islam.
rows.anchor: these people were never inflicted with the ailment of greed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When opponents speak foolishly, the believers disengage rather than debate, saying each side is responsible for its own deeds and may choose its path.
rows.anchor: When these people hear the nonsensical talk

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Peace be upon you” signals a polite parting, as in Abraham's words to his father; they leave because engagement with the ignorant brings no benefit.
rows.anchor: implies parting ways. It is similar to what Abraham

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'anic style lets a person's attitude stand in for spoken words; this expression occurs in several places.
rows.anchor: At times, a person’s attitude takes the place of his words.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here, hidāya means rightly guiding someone.
rows.anchor: to rightly guide someone. This sentence
